Right now I'm researching for an essay comparing Kubrick's The Shining with its Stephen King adaptation to TV and the subsequent Doctor Sleep novel and movie. 

Of all the many books and articles I've looked over in the past few days nothing is as illuminating as this analysis of King and Kubrick's differing visions of the story.

[https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2020/the-shining-at-40/king-vs-kubrick-the-origins-of-evil/](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2020/the-shining-at-40/king-vs-kubrick-the-origins-of-evil/)

I recommend you read it for insight into the themes of the story. 

I would differ with your interpretation in general, though you still make some valid points. I would consider that Kubrick didn't think of the evil represented by the hotel, the whole complex of "white man's burden"-Native burial ground-N-word slur as anachronistic but very defintely actual in his time and place. 

In other words I believe it's a little optimistic on your part to characterise the imperialist-racist dimension of the evil manifest in the hotel as something straight from the past. Nothing about today's society suggests it is.

In terms of Kubrick’s films, an anthropological understanding of human nature came first; a sociological and political understanding were secondary.  The supreme example of this is in “2001: A Space Odyssey,” where the the behaviors of the ape-men in the “Dawn of Man” portion of the film are still evident — expressed with subtlety, but even more dangerously — in the behaviors of humans in the year 2001.   Clan-based rivalries are writ large in the conflict between nationalities, namely the Americans and the Russians — when the Americans find the monolith, they think of it not as a find for all of humanity but as something to be kept secret for their rivals, with whom they compete for resources and hegemony, and with whom the potential for violent conflict is ever-present.   They are as protective over, as proprietary over that dug-up monolith as the ape-men were over their watering hole.  What if discovery of the monolith could give them an advantage over their enemies? What if their enemies’ discovery of the monolith could put them at a disadvantage?  “I’m sorry, Dr. Smislov, but I’m not at liberty to discuss it.” They need to know what they *have* before they can decide whether to share it.   It doesn’t belong to all humanity.  It belongs to them.

All of the spacecraft in 2001 are descendants of the first tool weapon; with it, humans explore and they conquer.  Also, it was because of intelligence that the bone cudgel was used as a weapon to kill; even in the Dawn of Man sequence, humanity’s evolutionary edge, that which made it a formidable predator, was its intelligence.  Enter HAL 9000, whose intelligence in principle surpasses that of his human makers.  Lying and deceit, dissembling is a form of weaponized intelligence, of *strategy* in the face of the rival or enemy,  that is alive and well in the world of 2001.    The Americans lead everyone, including the Russians, to believe that there is an epidemic at the base in order to hide the discovery of the monolith.   Floyd not only orchestrates this prudent deception, but also conceals from the Discovery crew the purpose of their mission.  Frank and Dave, in their conflict with their now would-be be predator, HAL 9000, try to outface each other in deception.   Using intelligence to distort information and to score an advantage.  “Say, Dave.  I’m having a problem.  I wonder if you might take a look at it with me.”  HAL, too, conceals information — not letting on that he knows anything about their plans to disconnect him.   Pretending everything is still normal and that they can continue to stay relatively unguarded.  He reveals himself to Dave only when Frank and the astronauts have been killed and he has Dave, locked outside the pod,  in a check-mate position.   The ape-men weaponized intelligence through technology.   That weaponization of intelligence is further refined in 2001 through applying intelligence towards the purpose of lying, deceit, dissembling in order to score an adversary advantage.

I mention this because the Dawn of Man sequence is foundational not only for the view of humanity in the rest of “2001,” but also for the rest of Kubrick’s films, period.   For example:

— the marauding droogs in “A Clockwork Orange” harken back to Moonwatcher and his cohorts preparing to raid the watering hole.  In the scene where Alex and his droogs begin to descend, with stealth, on Frank Alexander’s house, they even instinctively,  strategically, hunch their posture in a way reminiscent of the gait of the ape-men.  They climb, even (a simian skill not adumbrated by Kubrick in “2001,” but well-known to all). 

Alex’s cane — which he weaponizes, to strike blows — rests as “trustily” in his grip as the bone cudgel held by the ape-men.   Alex, too, knows how to weaponize humanize intelligence through deceit — “my friend’s lying in the middle of the road, bleeding to death.” But Alex’s mendacity is nothing compared to the scale on which the Minister of the Interior, and the government itself, orchestrates the smoke and mirrors of deceit and misinformation.

— in “Barry Lyndon,” there is the scene of the brutal attack on Bullingdon;  a genteel social gathering suddenly explodes into the chaos of a melee (or at least the semblance of one) as Barry attacks his stepson with arguably homicidal intent. The high society of 18th century England is hardly divorced from the world of the ape-men — still the tribalism of rebutting those who do not belong to their circle, those outsiders like Barry, the Irish peasant; still waging war, albeit by proxy (“very good, Mr. Barry, rouse another company too [of soldiers] and go with them”).  

— In “The Shining,” Jack regresses to much farther back than the 1920’s.   In his hunched gait — ostensibly due to his fall down the stairs — and his grunting, and his swinging of the ax, he resembles a simian predator right out of the Dawn of Man.  What he intends to do with that tool weapon, that ax, is kill his rival, even if that rival be his own son.  Kubrick had read Freud, who commented anthropologically not just on intra-species murder and on Homo sapiens’ proclivity for it, but also intra-familial murder (fathers against sons; sons against fathers).  Diane Johnson, who co-wrote the screenplay with Kubrick:  “A father threatening his son is compelling.  It’s a playing out of primal archetype.”   Kubrick also studied myths and was no doubt aware of Saturn, of Chronos, devouring his own children, who were his rivals for power.   By the time Jack chases Danny through the labyrinth, he’s not a man of the 1920’s, let alone the 1970’s.  He’s akin to a killer ape chasing a rival — no matter that it’s his own kith and kin— through a snowy wilderness.  Even his level of intelligence is simian, borderline proto-human — a vacuousness in his eyes as he almost bemusedly reasons out, wrongly, that — because the footprints have disappeared - Danny must be  close.

— in “Full Metal Jacket,” the recruits are being trained to kill and to develop a fusional relationship with their tool weapons.  Are we far, especially here, from the Dawn of Man sequence?  During the nighttime attack on Pyle, the recruits use that similar stealth of step, and hunched posture, that Alex and his droogs had used in Clockwork.   It is the gait of ambush, not dissimilar to Moon Watcher’s and cohorts’ raid of the watering hole.  

— in “Eyes Wide Shut,” even, you have band of brothers — possibly fraternity brothers — who are akin to Alex and his droogs as they roam the streets like would-be marauders.  Like Moonwatcher;  Alex;  Animal Mother.  *They* merely threaten, except for that initial shove.  But they feel the same underlying sense of full-throated well being as was referenced by the squad leader in FMJ who declared, cheerily, “We’re jolly green giants walking the earth, with guns.” It’s the same sense of intoxicated well-being — euphoric with power, if not with a sense of malevolent glee — that Moonwatcher must have felt in brazenly flinging his tool, his murder weapon, high into the air.  As if to say “who is there who will challenge me?

In this instance I would say The Shining borders on camp. It’s something you watch in college after 4 monster bong rips. That’s how I did it. I saw it as a guy who had writer’s block and probably alcoholic psychosis. A child who can send thoughts? It’s expensive gorgeous camp. Misery and Dolores Claiborne I can understand diving into. However The Shining is more like Cannonball Run. Or Scarface. Films famous for intriguing college potheads. They’re called stoner movies. A 1 and done. The guy goes crazy, there’s a psychic child…it’s a plot where you only have a limited time in your youth to enjoy it before you age out. Monster bong rips and Dr. Sleep at 40, I just turned it off. I think The Shining should be enjoyed young and at face value.

Yeah I agree that Kubrick focuses primarily on anthropological aspects rather than social and political ones. Yes Jack's hostility against his own son can be attributed to an animalistic primal instinct of self sustain. Though even if secondary, political and social issues are present in Kubrick's movie. Just like you said the rivalry between the Russians and Americans even though reflecting a deeper anthropological aspect can be described as a political-social issue. So I would argue that the murderous urge Jack has is only a Freudian mechanism deeply rooted inside human nature. Cold war era American children grew with the fear of communism. They learned to despise it. Being judged by others as a socialist-communist meant social exclusion. Social inclusion is a big part of self sustainability and social exclusion brings fear because of that. Just like the cold war child learnt to fear communism Jack learnt to fear social minorities, socially lower classes and ultimately personal failure (as a magnificent writer in his case). Failure is his predator. Though the nature of this predator is worse. His own mind is waging war against him. Leading to his total mental breakdown. Fear and anger are also heavily linked. They both are part of the fight or flight system that humans and most mammals have. Hence why he eventually turns against his own family. When flight is inevitable fight is the only way to go.
